questions.subject: social
questions.text: Well irrigation is the most important irrigation system. Illustrate.

answer.value: Well irrigation is the most important type of irrigation in India. Supplying ground water by digging or drilling wells is called well irrigation. It provides water to large areas of agricultural land, is more useful in low-rainfall regions, is easier to construct and maintain, and becomes essential where canals and tanks are not available. There are two types of wells - open wells and tube wells.

Construction and maintenance of wells is easier. Well irrigation becomes essential where the canals and tanks are not available. There are two types of wells: 1.Open wells 2. Tube wells.". The MQP prints no answer key; answer sourced from the textbook per review_policy_v1 §2-4.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: What were the causes and consequences of the Battle of Plassey?

answer.value: The Battle of Plassey (1757) was fought between the young Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah, and the British. Causes: (1) misuse of Dastaks by Company officials, which angered Siraj-ud-Daulah; (2) the British mending/fortifying the fort of Calcutta with cannons without permission; and (3) the Black Hole Tragedy, in which 123 of 146 imprisoned Englishmen died, enraging Robert Clive. Consequences: (1) the war exposed the immorality and lack of unity among Indians and the greed of Indian businessmen; (2) Mir Jaffar became the Nawab of Bengal; (3) the Company gained exclusive rights to trade in Bengal; and (4) Mir Jaffar had to pay Rupees seventeen crore seventy lakh as war indemnity to the British East India Company.

The company gained exclusive rights to trade in Bengal. 4. Mir Jaffar had to pay Rupees seventeen crores and seventy lakhs as war indemnity to the British East India Company.". questions.subject: social
questions.text: What were the effects of the British land tax system in India?

answer.value: The effects of the British Land Tax system were: (1) a new class of Zamindars who exploited the farmers was created; (2) the farmers subjected to the Zamindars' exploitation slowly became landless; (3) land became a commodity and loans could be raised by mortgaging land; (4) many Zamindars also had to mortgage their lands to pay the land taxes; (5) the agriculture sector became commercialized and had to grow raw materials needed by industries back in England; and (6) the money lenders became strong.

answer_provenance.basis: Textbook 10th English  SS  Part - 1 2026-27(Part 1), pdf p36 (printed p23): "The Impact of the British Land Tax system : 1. Loans could be raised by mortgaging the lands. 4. Many Zamindars also had to mortgage their lands in order to pay the land taxes. 5. The Agriculture sector became commercialized and had to grow raw materials needed by industries back in England. 6. The money lenders became strong.". The MQP prints no answer key; answer sourced from the textbook per review_policy_v1 §2-4.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: How are Evergreen forests different from Deciduous monsoon forests?

answer.value: Evergreen forests are found in regions not more than 900 m above sea level that receive an annual rainfall of more than 250 cm (e.g. the Western Ghats, the north-eastern states and the Andaman-Nicobar islands); since their trees are always green they are called evergreen forests. Deciduous monsoon forests are more widely distributed and are found in areas receiving 75 to 250 cm of rainfall; they form about 65.5% of the total forest area, and since India has mainly a monsoon climate they are distributed widely; their trees shed their leaves during the dry winters, so they are called deciduous monsoon forests.

answer_provenance.basis: Textbook 10th English  SS  Part - 1 2026-27(Part 1), pdf p119 (printed p106): "Evergreen forests: In India, evergreen forests are found in regions which are not more than 900 mts above sea level and receive an annual rainfall of more than 250 cms. ... Since the trees are always green they are called Evergreen forests. Deciduous monsoon forests : This type of forest is more widely distributed in India. They are seen in areas receiving 75 to 250 cms of rainfall. It forms about 65.5% of the total area of forests. ... The trees shed their leaves during the dry winters. As such these are also called deciduous monsoon forests.". The MQP prints no answer key; answer sourced from the textbook per review_policy_v1 §2-4.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: How is Global Positioning system useful?

answer.value: The main objective of the Global Positioning System (GPS) is to indicate the location of a stationary or moving object or person by pointing out its latitude, longitude and height above sea level. It works on the basis of information sent by more than 20 artificial satellites and an individual's receiver set on the earth's surface. Today it is very useful in many areas - for locating and tracking stationary and moving objects, navigation and related applications.

questions.text: Explain the role of the Panchayat Raj Institutions in Rural Development.

answer.value: Panchayat Raj institutions play a major role in enabling rural people to participate in rural development. questions.subject: social
questions.text: Explain the differences between Personal finance and Public Finance.

answer.value: Personal Finance deals with the income, expenditure and debt management of an individual or a family - balancing income and expenditure to achieve progress (and when expenditure exceeds income, it leads to debt). answer.value: An entrepreneur has to perceive opportunities, plan, organise resources and oversee production and marketing, motivate assistants, and above all innovate and bear risk. questions.subject: social
questions.text: Explain the effects of arms race.

answer.value: An arms race is the competition among countries for the production, stockpiling and use of arms. Its effects (disadvantages) are: it increases fear and instability among countries and raises the possibility of war; it hinders the achievement of world peace; and it leads to financial loss and economic instability, diverting resources away from constructive use.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: Mention the differences between the workers of Organised and Unorganised sector.

answer.value: Organised workers are those who work in specific fields governed by legal rules and regulations; their work is subject to specific terms and conditions, there is an organizational hierarchy, their transactions are recorded in writing, and they get fixed wages, allowances, paid leave, pension and medical facilities and fixed working hours (e.g. workers in insurance companies, educational institutions, banks, armed forces, private companies and government departments). Unorganised workers are those who work in areas not governed by specific rules, regulations or unions and who earn daily wages or material benefits; the unorganised sector is very vast and not under government control (e.g. domestic servants, construction workers, agricultural labourers, footpath hawkers, vehicle repairers and push-cart vegetable vendors).

Since the unorganized sector is very vast, it is not under government control. For ex: domestic servants, construction workers, agricultural labours, footpath hawkers, vehicle repairers, push-cart vegetable vendors etc.". questions.subject: social
questions.text: Explain the methods followed by the Revolutionaries in the freedom struggle of India.

answer.value: The revolutionaries dreamt of a totally free India and strongly believed that the British could be thrown out of India only by violent means. The methods they followed included: establishing secret branches/societies in India and abroad; collecting money and arms and training people; forming organizations such as the 'Anusheelana Samithi' and 'Abhinava Bharata'; using bombs and firearms to achieve their objectives; and spreading their ideas through publications. The government tried hard to suppress them - many were arrested for murder attempts and given life imprisonment, and many were hanged to death. Prominent revolutionary leaders were V.D. Savarkar, Aurobindo Ghosh, Shyamji Krishna Verma, Madam Cama, Khudiram Bose, Ramaprasad Bismil, Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekar Azad.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: Explain the role of Raja Ram Mohan Roy in the Social and religious reform movement of India.

answer.value: Raja Ram Mohan Roy was one of the important persons in the establishment of the Brahmo Samaj and has been called 'The Father of Indian Renaissance'. He was well-versed in many languages (Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian, English, French, Greek and Latin) and had studied the principles of Hinduism, Islam, Sufism, Christianity and Buddhism. He studied the Upanishads and questioned the practice of idol-worship, and argued that modern science and English education were essential for an Indian revival. He opposed the exploitation of women and led an organized attack against the practices of sati and child marriage, supporting the Prohibition of Sati Act introduced by Lord William Bentinck. He also tried to develop rationalism among people through journalism, starting a newspaper in Bengali.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: List out the features of Black soil.

answer.value: The features of Black soil are: it is also called 'Regur soil'; it is best suited for cotton cultivation and so is also called 'Black Cotton soil'; the area of black soil is called the Deccan Trap; it is formed from the weathering of igneous rock; it contains more clay particles; it is fertile and capable of retaining water; it is seen in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, western Andhra Pradesh and north Karnataka; it contains more lime and magnesium carbonates and is highly suitable for dry farming; and the major crops grown on it are cotton, jowar, wheat, onion, chilli, tobacco, oil seeds, lemon and grapes.

questions.subject: social
questions.text: Explain the causes and effects of the Third Anglo-Mysore war.

answer.value: The main cause of the Third Anglo-Mysore War was the political situation of Travancore: the king of Travancore built a fort in Kochi with British help and captured the Ayacotta and Kanganoor forts from the Dutch, which was a clear breach of the Mangalore Treaty. In the war the British under General Meadows captured Karwar, Coimbatore and Dindigul; Tippu Sultan captured Sathyamangalam but failed to take Thiruchanapalli; then Lord Cornwallis took over the British command, captured Kolar, Hosakote and Bangalore (destroying its fort), and sought the help of the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad. The combined army marched to Srirangapattana in 1792 and destroyed the fort. As an effect, Tippu Sultan was forced to sign the 'Treaty of Srirangapatna' in 1792 on unfavourable conditions, being forced to part with half of his territory, and with this the Third Anglo-Mysore War came to an end.
